questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Discuss the processes by which River Sanaga erodes and transports its load.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A river such as the Sanaga does its work in two linked ways: it **erodes** (wears away the bed and banks and breaks up rock and sediment) and it **transports** the material that results (its **load**). Both depend on the **velocity and discharge** of the water, which are greatest in flood, when most of the work is done.

**1. Processes of erosion**

| Process | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic action** | The force of moving water alone pushes into cracks, joints and bedding planes in the bed and banks; air trapped in the cracks is compressed and released (**cavitation**), so the rock is loosened and pieces are plucked out. It is strong at rapids, waterfalls and river bends. |
| **Abrasion (corrasion)** | Pebbles, sand and boulders carried by the current are hurled and rolled against the bed and banks, grinding, scouring and cutting them like sandpaper. It produces **potholes** and deepens the channel; it is the most important erosive process in a river carrying a coarse load. |
| **Attrition** | The particles of the load knock against each other and against the bed, so they are broken, rounded and made smaller and smoother downstream. This reduces the load but does not erode the channel itself. |
| **Solution (corrosion)** | Slightly acid river water dissolves soluble rocks (limestone, rock salt) and soluble minerals, and the ions go into solution. |

Erosion is **vertical** (downcutting of the bed, mainly in the steep upper course, giving V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls) and **lateral** (sideways cutting of the banks, mainly on the outside of meander bends in the lower course, giving a wide floodplain).

**2. Processes of transport**

| Process | What is moved |
|---|---|
| **Solution** | Dissolved ions (calcium, bicarbonate, etc.) carried invisibly in the water. |
| **Suspension** | Fine particles (clay, silt, fine sand) are held up by the turbulence of the water and give the river a muddy colour; this is the largest part of the load in many rivers. |
| **Saltation** | Medium sand and fine gravel are lifted for a short time, travel in a series of hops and fall back to the bed. |
| **Traction** (rolling, sliding, dragging) | The coarsest particles (large pebbles and boulders) are pushed along the bed in floods; with saltation, they make up the **bed load**. |

**3. Controls.** The size of particle moved depends on velocity (the Hjulstrom relationship): fine sand is eroded at low velocity, but clay and silt, because they stick together, need a higher velocity to be picked up and stay in suspension even when velocity drops; coarse gravel needs a high velocity. When the velocity falls (where the gradient decreases, at a bend, a lake or the sea), the river **deposits** its load, largest particles first, and the load becomes the sediment of bars, floodplains and deltas.

*Marking idea: about four marks for erosion processes (each named and explained) and four for transport processes.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) The table below shows the particle size (mm) and percentage weight of samples A and B.

| PARTICLE SIZE (mm) | % WEIGHT OF SAMPLE A | % WEIGHT OF SAMPLE B |
|---|---|---|
| 2 - 1 | 10 | 10 |
| 1 - 1/2 | 18 | 85 |
| 1/2 - 1/4 | 37 | 05 |
| 1/4 - 1/8 | 20 | - |
| 1/8 - 1/16 | 15 | - |

(i) Draw a histogram for Sample A. (4 marks)

(ii) Establish a cumulative frequency curve for Sample B. (5 marks)

(iii) Suggest the environment of formation of Sample B. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Check of the data.** Sample A: 10 + 18 + 37 + 20 + 15 = 100 %. Sample B: 10 + 85 + 5 = 100 %. The classes are the usual sand grades (Wentworth scale), each half the size of the one before: 2-1 mm very coarse sand, 1-1/2 mm coarse sand, 1/2-1/4 mm medium sand, 1/4-1/8 mm fine sand, 1/8-1/16 mm very fine sand.

**(i) Histogram for Sample A (4 marks)**

Data to plot:

| Class (mm) | 2-1 | 1-1/2 | 1/2-1/4 | 1/4-1/8 | 1/8-1/16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| % weight | 10 | 18 | 37 | 20 | 15 |

How to draw it:

- Draw two axes. **Horizontal axis**: the five particle-size classes in order (from coarse, 2-1 mm, on the left to fine, 1/8-1/16 mm, on the right, or the reverse), labelled "Particle size (mm)". The classes halve in size each time, so on this geometric (phi) scale every class has the **same width** and the bars are drawn equally wide and touching.
- **Vertical axis**: "% weight of sample A", from 0 to 40 with an even scale (for example 5 % per division).
- Draw touching rectangles of heights **10, 18, 37, 20 and 15**, and give the graph a title ("Histogram of particle size, Sample A").
- The histogram has its **tallest bar (37 %) at the medium-sand class** and a spread of between 10 and 20 % in the four other classes: the sediment is a **mixture** of grades (the sample is only moderately sorted).

Marks: title and labelled axes with scale (1), correct bar heights (2), neat touching bars of equal width (1).

**(ii) Cumulative frequency curve for Sample B (5 marks)**

A cumulative curve shows the **percentage of the sample that is finer than a given size**. Add the percentages starting from the finest class, and plot each total against the **upper size limit** of its class:

| Size limit (mm) | Cumulative % finer than this size |
|---|---|
| 1/4 | 0 |
| 1/2 | 5 |
| 1 | 5 + 85 = 90 |
| 2 | 90 + 10 = 100 |

Drawing: horizontal axis = particle size (mm) on a **logarithmic scale** (or on an equal-interval scale of the classes, since each class is half the previous one); vertical axis = cumulative % from 0 to 100. Plot the four points and join them with a smooth S-shaped curve; the curve is **very steep between 1/2 and 1 mm** and flat before and after it. (If the percentages are added from the coarse end instead, the points are 2 mm: 0 %; 1 mm: 10 %; 1/2 mm: 95 %; 1/4 mm: 100 % and the curve is the mirror image; either direction is accepted if the axis is labelled.)

Reading the curve (log interpolation between the plotted points; values to be checked on the candidate's own graph):

- median size (50 %) is about **0.72 mm** (coarse sand);
- first quartile (25 %) is about 0.59 mm and third quartile (75 %) is about 0.89 mm;
- Trask sorting coefficient $S_0=\sqrt{Q_3/Q_1}=\sqrt{0.885/0.589}\approx 1.2$, which is close to 1, so the sample is **very well sorted**. (For comparison, Sample A gives a median of about 0.33 mm and $S_0\approx 1.8$: **moderately well to well sorted**, much less uniform than B.)

Marks: both axes correctly labelled and scaled (2), cumulative values correct (2), smooth curve (1).

**(iii) Environment of formation of Sample B (2 marks)**

About 85 % of the sample is a single grade (coarse sand, 1-1/2 mm) with practically no fine silt or clay, and very little coarse material: the sediment is **very well sorted and clean (fines winnowed out)**. This is typical of a **high-energy, steady and persistently reworking environment** in which the fine material is washed or blown away: most likely a **beach (swash zone) deposit**; a **wind-blown (aeolian) sand** or a well-washed **river channel bar** are also possible. A beach is the best single answer because the coarse sand needs strong, repeated wave action.

**(i) Sphericity (2 marks).** Sphericity is a measure of **how closely the overall shape of a grain approaches that of a sphere**; it describes the **form** of the grain, that is, the relation between its three axes (a longest, b intermediate, c shortest), and it **does not depend on how sharp the corners are**. A cube-shaped grain with sharp corners and a smooth rounded disc can have a similar sphericity. Wadell's true sphericity is (volume of the grain / volume of the smallest sphere that encloses it) to the power 1/3; a simple form used in sedimentology is the Krumbein sphericity, $(bc/a^2)^{1/3}$, which equals 1 for a sphere and is smaller for rod-like or disc-like grains. Elongated, flat grains have low sphericity. It is controlled mainly by the **original shape** and the cleavage or bedding of the parent rock, and only little by distance of transport.

**(ii) Roundness (2 marks).** Roundness is a measure of **the sharpness (smoothness) of the corners and edges of a grain**, whatever its overall shape. Wadell's roundness is the average radius of curvature of the corners divided by the radius of the largest circle that fits inside the grain; a perfect sphere has a value of 1, and sharp-cornered grains have values near 0. In practice grains are placed into classes by visual comparison (Powers' chart): **very angular, angular, sub-angular, sub-rounded, rounded, well rounded**. Roundness **increases with distance and time of transport** (abrasion and attrition during river, beach or wind transport; wind-blown grains are the best rounded), so it indicates how far and by what agent a grain travelled and whether it has been reworked.

**(iii) Maturity (2 marks).** Maturity (of a sediment, mostly sandstone) is **the degree to which a sediment has been changed by weathering, transport and reworking towards its stable "end product"**. Two kinds are recognised:

- **Textural maturity**: the removal of clay and fine matrix, improvement in **sorting** and increase in **roundness** of grains; classes are *immature* (clay-rich, poorly sorted, angular), *submature*, *mature* (clay-free, but moderately sorted) and *supermature* (clay-free, well sorted and well rounded).
- **Mineralogical maturity**: the loss of unstable minerals (feldspar, mica, ferromagnesian minerals and rock fragments) so that only the most resistant mineral, **quartz** (with zircon, tourmaline, rutile), remains; a high quartz/(feldspar + rock fragments) ratio shows a mature sediment. A quartz arenite is mineralogically supermature, an arkose or a greywacke is immature.

A mature sediment has therefore been through long, energetic transport or repeated reworking in a **stable, humid or high-energy** setting (for example beach or aeolian sand); an immature one was deposited quickly and near its source (alluvial fan, turbidite).
